data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without induction by re-framing 'preference' as a non-epistemic, methodological rule for selecting the most falsifiable survivor, not as a bet on future truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent acts on the theory expecting it to succeed in practical application rather than to fail under test, induction is smuggled in.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies the theory is 'closer to the truth' in a probabilistic sense, the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'corroboration as probability' (which Popper rejects) and 'corroboration as a report of past performance.' The preference is rational not because it predicts future success (induction), but because the better-corroborated theory has withstood more severe tests, making it the best available target for further attempts at falsification. Acting on it is simply choosing the strongest link in the chain of knowledge to stress-test next.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
